text: In case of a snakebite: keep the victim still, wash with soap and water, and go to the hospital. NEVER use a tourniquet.
The rattlesnake only uses its rattle as a warning — never as provocation. It prefers to avoid confrontation.
The jararaca snake's venom was essential in creating Captopril, a medication that controls high blood pressure.
FIRST AID: Wash the bite area with soap and water and cover with a clean cloth. Go to a hospital immediately.
The snake's forked tongue 'smells' the air — each tip captures particles from different directions.
Of the 400 snake species in Brazil, only 70 are venomous. Most are harmless!
FIRST AID: Don't take home remedies like Mercurochrome or vodka on the bite. Only a hospital can provide proper treatment.
The mussurana is known as the 'good snake' because it feeds on venomous snakes like jararacas.
Snakes don't have eyelids — their eyes are covered by a transparent scale that sheds along with their skin.
JARARACA BITE (Bothrops): severe pain, swelling and bleeding at the site. Lay the victim down, keep the limb at rest and get to a hospital. The antivenom is antibotropic.
The anaconda can stay submerged for hours with only its eyes and nostrils above water, waiting for prey.
The rattlesnake's rattle gains a new segment with each skin shed — it doesn't indicate the snake's exact age.
RATTLESNAKE BITE (Crotalus): the site barely hurts, but double vision, drooping eyelids and dark urine show up. It is serious - go to a hospital even without pain. Anticrotalic serum.
Snakes aren't slimy! Their skin is dry, smooth, and covered with keratin scales.
If you find a snake in the wild, keep your distance. It will flee — that's exactly what it wants.
BUSHMASTER BITE (Lachesis): combines pain and swelling with neurological symptoms. It is the most severe snake accident in Brazil. Go to a hospital immediately.
The true coral snake has neurotoxic venom — one of the most potent in the world. But it's docile and avoids humans.
Boa constrictors have no venom. They kill by constriction: wrapping around prey and squeezing until breathing stops.
Antivenom is free through Brazil's public health system (SUS) and is available at referral hospitals. The sooner the treatment, the better the outcome.
Each snake has a unique pattern of scales on its head — like a fingerprint!
Killing snakes is an environmental crime (Law 9,605/98). They are protected by law throughout Brazil.
The bushmaster is the only viper in the Americas that lays eggs. All others (jararaca, rattlesnake) are viviparous.
Snakes control rat populations — without them, we'd have many more diseases like leptospirosis.
Loreal pits (between eyes and nostrils) allow jararacas to 'see' the heat of prey in the dark.
The name 'urutu' comes from Tupi-Guarani and means 'snake that bites'.
The caninana can climb vertical trees with ease to hunt bird nests.
Snakes don't drink milk! This myth arose because they enter barns looking for rodents.
The vine snake is so thin that it camouflages perfectly among branches — almost impossible to see.
Anti-venom serum is produced from antibodies of horses immunized with snake venom.
False corals imitate the colors of true corals to deceive predators — this is called Batesian mimicry.
Snakes shed their skin several times a year. Young snakes shed more than adults because they grow faster.
A boa constrictor can live over 30 years in captivity with proper care.
Rattlesnake venom can cause double vision — one of the neurological symptoms of crotalic envenomation.
The largest venomous snake in the Americas is the bushmaster, which can reach 3 meters in length.
Snakes are essential for ecological balance: they control pests and serve as food for birds of prey.
Respect snakes. They've been on Earth for over 100 million years and are fundamental to nature.
PREVENTION: When walking in forest areas, wear long pants and closed boots. Stepping on a snake is the main cause of accidents.
FIRST AID: In case of a bite, keep the victim calm and still. Remove rings and tight clothing before swelling occurs.
DON'T apply a tourniquet, cut the bite area, or suck the venom — this worsens the condition and can cause infection.
PREVENTION: Never put your hands in holes, crevices, or under rocks without checking first. Many snakes hide there.
PREVENTION: At home, keep gardens trimmed and free of debris. Snakes seek shelter in places with hiding spots.
FIRST AID: Note the time of the bite and, if possible, take a photo of the snake. This helps the doctor choose the right serum.
PREVENTION: At night, use a flashlight when walking in poorly lit areas. Snakes are more active at dusk and nighttime.
PREVENTION: If you find a snake at home, don't try to grab it with your hands. Call the fire department (193) for safe removal.
TRUE CORAL BITE (Micrurus): the mark can be almost invisible and painless. It is still an emergency - the venom gradually paralyses the body. Antielapidic serum.
BITE FROM A NON-VENOMOUS SNAKE (boa, anaconda, tiger rat snake, mussurana): there is no venom, but the bite can get infected. Wash it well and check that your tetanus shot is up to date.
WHAT NEVER TO DO with a bite: tourniquet, cutting, piercing, sucking the venom out, applying ice, kerosene, alcohol or tobacco. All of that only makes it worse.
If you are bitten, drink water, stay calm and do not run. Exertion spreads the venom faster through the body.
In case of a snake accident call the Poison Information Center: 0800 722 6001. It gives guidance 24 hours a day.
PREVENTION: anyone working in fields or forest should wear leather leg guards or tall boots. It is the gear that prevents the most bites.
PREVENTION: check the spot before putting on shoes, stacking firewood or moving piles of debris. Snakes like dark, warm places.
PREVENTION: rats and garbage attract snakes. Keep food stored and trash well sealed - without rodents, they have no reason to come inside.
PREVENTION: always walk on the open trail, never through dense brush or over dry leaves. That way you see where you step.
PREVENTION: when camping, keep the tent away from fallen logs and rocks. Shake out your shoes and sleeping bag before use.
PREVENTION: if a snake shows up, stop and back away slowly. It only strikes when cornered or stepped on. Running or trying to kill it is the biggest risk.
A snake's heart has three chambers and can shift inside the body when it swallows a large prey.
After a big meal, a snake can go months without eating: its metabolism slows down a lot.
The jararaca is the snake that causes the most accidents in Brazil, simply because it lives close to people.
Snakes have no outer ear: they feel vibrations in the ground through the bones of the jaw.
Jacobson's organ, in the roof of the mouth, analyses the particles the tongue brings in. That is their sense of smell.
The anaconda is the largest snake in Brazil and can grow past 6 metres.
A snake sheds its whole skin at once, including the clear covering over the eyes.
The rattle is made of keratin, the same material as our nails and hair.
The true coral snake is gentle: it only bites if it is squeezed or stepped on.
The boa constrictor has labial pits that detect the body heat of prey even in the dark.
Snakes swallow prey whole, without chewing: all the digestion is chemical.
A snake's stomach acid is strong enough to dissolve bone.
The jararaca's strike is faster than the human eye can follow.
The mussurana is immune to the venom of other snakes and feeds on them.
The vine snake is so thin it looks like a twig: many people walk right past it.
Snakes are cold-blooded: they depend on the environment to control their body temperature.
The caninana puffs up its neck when it feels threatened, to look bigger.
Baby rattlesnakes are born with working venom and rattle.
The bushmaster is the largest venomous viper in the Americas, reaching 3 metres.
Snakes control rodents and, by doing so, help reduce diseases such as leptospirosis.
A snake's skeleton can have more than 300 vertebrae, each with a pair of ribs.
The forked tongue gives a sense of direction: each tip picks up scent from one side.
Some snakes can glide between branches by flattening their body into a ribbon shape.
The rattlesnake's scientific name, Crotalus durissus, was given by Linnaeus in 1758.
Sea snakes spend their whole lives in the ocean and must surface to breathe.
Shedding is a sign of growth: young snakes shed several times a year.
Snake skin is dry and smooth. The feeling of slime is a myth.
Snakes see poorly when things are still, but they notice any movement very well.
Some species imitate the true coral snake pattern: they are the false coral snakes.
Night snakes usually have vertical pupils; day snakes have round ones.
